005 
Caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia for a patient 
with stiff person syndrome 
A. Forbes and V. Skelton 
Kings College Hospital, London 
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare disorder characterised by involuntary activation of the 
motor unit leading to episodic severe muscle spasms and stiffness classically affecting axial and 
proximal lower-limb musculature. Spasms may be triggered by various stimuli including pain. 
Prolonged muscle weakness has been described after volatile anaesthesia and muscle relaxant 
administration in people with SPS [1]. 
Description 
A 39-year-old woman with SPS presented for caesarean section at 39+1 weeks gestation. The 
diagnosis of SPS had been made 18 years previously following episodes of spasms leading to 
convulsions. Investigations excluded epilepsy, but she was found to have anti-glutamic acid 
decarboxylase antibodies. Spasms were managed with diazepam 2 mg as required. She was 
concerned that labour might precipitate spasms, so had elected for caesarean delivery. Consent 
for spinal anaesthesia was obtained and the possibility of prolonged ventilation in the unlikely 
event of general anaesthesia discussed. In theatre, intravenous (IV) access was secured and 
standard monitoring applied. After skin infiltration with 1% lidocaine, 2.3 ml of 0.5% hyperbaric 
bupivacaine and 300 µg of diamorphine were injected intrathecally through a 25 g pencil point 
needle. Bilateral sensory block to T4 was achieved. The block was adequate throughout surgery 
and the baby was delivered uneventfully. IV paracetamol and per rectal diclofenac were given 
and regular oral analgesia was prescribed for the postoperative period. Ongoing management 
was discussed with a consultant neurologist and a breastfeeding pharmacist. Diazepam and its 
active metabolites pass into breast milk, causing sedation in the neonate, therefore baclofen was 
prescribed for spasms as required. Baclofen can also pass into breast milk but in sufficiently low 
amounts for it to be safe in breastfeeding; however, it can reduce milk supply. 
Discussion 
Pain can trigger spasms in patients with SPS, hence the decision to avoid labour, and ensure 
good postoperative pain relief. Symptomatic spasms may improve during pregnancy, but worsen 
again after delivery, so a plan for management needs to be in place [2]. As prolonged hypotonia 
and poor respiratory effort has been reported after general anaesthesia, spinal anaesthesia was 
preferred. There are previous reports of epidural analgesia and anaesthesia in parturients, but not 
spinal anaesthesia [2]. Our case gives evidence that spinal anaesthesia can be safely used for 
caesarean delivery.

References 
1. Sidransky MA, Tran NV, Kaye AD. Anaesthesia considerations in stiff person 
syndrome. Middle East Journal of Anaesthesiology 2013; 22: 217–21. 
2. Esch ME, Newsome SD. Improvement of stiff-person syndrome symptoms in 
pregnancy. Neurology Neuroimmunology and neuroinflammation 2020; 7: e684. 
Approvals
